notes.meaning: Moses calls on heaven and earth to listen as he begins his song. Creation itself is summoned to witness God's faithfulness and to hear the serious warning given to Israel. Because nature quietly obeys its Creator while people often rebel, heaven and earth stand as lasting witnesses.

Moses compares his teaching to gentle rain and morning dew falling on tender grass. Just as soft water revives the dry earth and helps crops grow, God's message is meant to soften hardened hearts and produce good fruit in those who receive it.
Moses announces that he will proclaim the character and great deeds of the Lord. He urges everyone listening to join him in honoring God's supreme majesty and goodness.

God is described as the Rock, showing that He is completely strong, faithful, and unchanging. Everything He does is perfect, and all His dealings with humanity are guided by true justice without any fault.

Moses contrasts God's blameless character with the twisted behavior of the people. Israel had stained themselves with sin and idolatry, acting like a crooked generation rather than true, obedient children of God.

Moses challenges the people for their foolish ingratitude toward the Lord. God acted as their Father and Creator, rescuing them from slavery and establishing them as a special nation. Turning their backs on Him after receiving such love was senseless and deeply wrong.

The people are told to look back at ancient history and learn from earlier generations. By asking their parents and elders, they would discover God's steady care throughout the past, reminding them of His faithfulness.

Long ago, when the Most High divided humanity into nations, He established their borders with Israel in mind. In His sovereign plan, God set aside the land of Canaan so there would be ample room for the tribes of Israel to dwell.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars follow readings found in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the ancient Greek Septuagint, which say 'sons of God' or 'angels of God,' suggesting that heavenly beings were allotted oversight of the other nations.

notes.meaning: Even though the entire world belongs to God, He selected Israel to be His prized possession. Out of pure grace, the Lord chose Jacob's descendants as His special inheritance to enjoy a close covenant bond with Him.

God found Israel in a dry, howling wilderness filled with danger and wild beasts. He encircled the people with His care, taught them His laws, and guarded them as tenderly as someone protects the pupil of their own eye.

God's care is compared to a mother eagle helping her young learn to fly. She nudges them from the nest, hovers close by, and catches them on her wings to protect them, just as the Lord carried Israel safely through hard times.

The Lord alone guided Israel safely on their journey, without any aid from foreign gods. Because no idol had any part in rescuing or providing for them, the Lord alone deserved their full loyalty and worship.

God brought Israel into a high, fertile country and gave them victory over strong mountain fortresses. He provided rich abundance from places that seemed barren, giving them wild honey found in rocky cliffs and olive oil from rugged hillsides.

Moses lists the rich food God gave the nation, such as butter, milk, and healthy livestock from the lush pastures of Bashan. The people enjoyed the best wheat and drank delicious wine made from the juice of choice grapes.

Israel is given the poetic name Jeshurun, which means upright, to highlight how far they fell from their calling. After enjoying great prosperity and abundance, the people became proud and unruly, like a pampered animal that kicks its master and abandons the God who saved it.

The people provoked God's jealousy and anger by turning away to worship detestable foreign idols. Just as unfaithfulness in marriage wounds a loyal spouse, Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness deeply offended the Lord who had loved them.

Israel offered sacrifices to demons rather than to the true God. They began worshipping newly invented deities that were powerless, unknown to their ancestors, and completely incapable of helping them.
Moses laments that Israel neglected the mighty Rock who had given them life. They forgot the loving God who formed them into a people and sustained them every step of the way.

When the Lord saw His people chasing after worthless idols, He turned away from them in deep anger. Because they were His own adopted sons and daughters, their betrayal was especially painful and deserving of judgment.

God declared that He would hide His face from them, withdrawing His favor and protection to see what their rebellion would produce. He described them as a stubborn and untrustworthy generation who refused to stay faithful to His covenant.

Israel had provoked God by running after things that were not real gods, so the Lord warned He would provoke them by favoring people who were not considered a nation. The apostle Paul later explained that this pointed to the gospel being welcomed by the Gentiles, prompting Israel to jealousy.

God's righteous wrath is pictured as a raging fire that burns down to the deepest realm of the dead. This fierce judgment would sweep across the land, ruining crops and scorching the foundations of the mountains.

The Lord warned that He would bring disaster upon disaster against those who abandoned Him. He compares His coming judgments—such as war, sickness, and famine—to a shower of deadly arrows shot from His bow.

The coming judgment would bring intense hunger, scorching fevers, and deadly sicknesses. Dangerous wild animals and venomous crawling snakes would also be sent against the people as part of their discipline.

War and devastation would strike the nation from all sides, bringing the terror of invading swords outside and overwhelming fear inside their homes. This judgment would spare no one, falling on young men, young women, little infants, and elderly people alike.

The Lord stated that Israel's persistent sins deserved complete destruction and being wiped out from human memory. Yet God held back from erasing them entirely so that their enemies would not wrongly boast that their own strength had conquered Israel.
